## Adjacent quiz-record independence when the same demonstrative slot is reused

- If a single supplied context line or paragraph contains two or more Jeopardy-style, quiz-style, or flashcard clue sentences that reuse the same pro-form or demonstrative slot (for example `this instrument`, `this work`, `this person`, or `this term`) for different answer targets, treat each clue sentence independently. Match the exact text after `Question:` against the clue sentence containing all of its descriptive predicates, not merely the shared pronoun or category word.
- Do not answer with the target of an earlier or adjacent sentence just because it sits next to the matching sentence in the same paragraph or because it uses the same `this X` wording. A candidate that satisfies a neighboring clue but fails one content word or relation in the current question is a distractor.
- For part/component, variant, or version patterns such as `The [regional/variant] version of this [instrument/object] has A, B, and C`, require the chosen candidate's context span to associate the candidate with the stated variant or version and all listed parts, components, or characteristics. Return the whole base category or entity named by that satisfying span. If the only nearby candidate satisfying the shared pro-form lacks those components, continue to the candidate whose context span explicitly lists them.
- Before finalizing, restate only the current question with adjacent quiz lines removed, and verify that every descriptor in the current question, especially listed parts, variants, dates, roles, or locations, is directly supported by the same context span as the candidate.

## Full fixed titles over supplied class synonyms

- When the question asks for the name given to a created work, publication, organization, or product and the source defines it with a full fixed title that includes a category/title suffix such as `Magazine`, `Journal`, `Press`, `Company`, or similar, return that full fixed title exactly as written. Do not truncate the title to a base term.
- The slot-refilling reduction removes a word only when the question already supplies that same word or class noun as a separate clue word. A near-synonym or different class word in the question, for example a question saying `journal` while the source title is `... magazine`, is not the supplied title word and does not justify dropping the source title suffix.
- Before applying any reduction, check whether the candidate is a proper name or fixed title used contiguously in the source. If it is, keep the full fixed title; if the candidate is a common noun with a removable classifier, reduce only the exact supplied class word.
- Preserve source capitalization, spelling, and word order.

## Declarative pronoun or possessive statements are cloze items, not yes/no questions

- If the text after `Question:` is a declarative statement containing a pronoun or possessive determiner such as `his`, `her`, `its`, `their`, `this`, or `these` and no explicit question word or blank, treat that pronoun or possessive as the missing slot even when the statement is syntactically complete. Resolve it to the named entity in the supplied context that directly satisfies the descriptive clause and return that entity's canonical name or title exactly as written.
- Do not answer `Yes`, `No`, `True`, or `False` for this question-answering skill, even if the statement could be interpreted as a proposition to verify. The task format is short-answer extraction, and a declarative fact with a pronoun is an identification cloze.
- For possessive determiners such as `his 1983 album`, `her book`, or `its founder`, find the most directly related context sentence that binds the possession or creation to a named person or entity, and return that associated person or entity rather than the work, object, or statement.
- If multiple entity names appear, use the possessive relation and all descriptive constraints in the statement to choose the owner, creator, author, or source named by that possessive, not a name merely mentioned nearby.
- Preserve exact capitalization, spelling, and source form.

## Indefinite-article and count-form matching for singular definitional and `one of these` slots

- When a prompt contains an indefinite article or the singular counter `one` (patterns such as `this, an X`, `an X in ...`, or `one of these Y`), parse the supplied foreign, local, or category term as a key and return the shortest base common noun from the directly defining equivalence (`X means Y`, `called Y`, `defined as Y`, or `one of these Y`). Retain the indefinite article when the completed slot is a singular count noun.
- Do not replace that base noun with a longer modified phrase found nearby, such as `white Y`, `Y of Z`, or a full proper-noun phrase, unless the prompt explicitly requests that modifier or full proper title. An answer that adds an unasked modifier or repeats a supplied class word is over-extracted.
- For an overt `one of these Y` slot, do not return a plural source form merely because the context mentions the category in the plural. The counter `one` requires a singular count noun; reconstruct the answer as `a/an Y`, not `Ys`.
- Preserve exact source spelling and capitalization. This rule refines the plural-source preservation rule only for overt `one of these` and indefinite-article definitional slots.

## Role/office constraints override quoted phrase overlap in person-identification clues

- When a declarative or demonstrative clue names a role, office, title, or status together with a quoted or largely repeated phrase, treat the phrase as surface evidence only. First collect every person candidate who holds the required role/status/office in the supplied context and satisfies the remaining location, party, organization, or date conditions.
- Do not answer with a person merely because that person is quoted saying or writing a phrase that matches the question's expression. A quoted speaker or writer is a distractor unless the same context also binds that person to the office/role/status required by the clue.
- Prefer the person whose defining or title-bearing context span directly joins the requested office/role/status with the other constraints. If the phrase match and the role evidence point to different people, discard the phrase match.
- For emphasis phrases such as "first and foremost," do not use the emphasis tokens as the primary selector. They often appear in direct quotations by a different person; the actual answer is the person described by the entire clause, not the speaker of the matching quote.

## Definitional/etymological variant and full-title component selection

- When a prompt supplies a definitional or etymological relation such as `whose name means ...`, `Greek for ...`, or `from ...`, and the supplied context contains multiple spelling or capitalization variants of the same term, select the exact form used in the context sentence that directly contains that definitional or etymological relation. Do not default to the first document heading, title-case headword, or alphabetically earlier alternative.
- Prefer the body-sentence form that immediately precedes or follows the parenthetical meaning, such as `X (... meaning '...')`, over the same term appearing in document titles, alt-name lists, or separate definitions. Preserve lowercase or title case exactly as in that direct body sentence, not as in the document title.
- If the prompt quotes a trailing component of a proper noun or fixed title by saying `this "Component"` or `about this "Component"`, treat the quoted component as a pointer to the full proper title, not as a supplied class word to remove. Return the complete proper title as a contiguous source span, including any leading article such as `The` or `A` and source punctuation, rather than reducing it to only the modifier before the quoted word.
- Do not apply slot-refilling reduction to remove a quoted word when the completed slot is a full proper title. For work, book, film, and other formal-name slots, the short-answer slot is the full title or name, not just the missing modifier; choose the source span that places the quoted component inside that full title. This overrides the usual remove-supplied-class-word reduction for quoted title components.

## Exact predicate matching over surface prominence in demonstrative/visual clues

- For clues with a visual or situational demonstrative such as `seen here`, `shown here`, `this food`, `this object`, or `this [class]`, first collect every candidate in the context that is directly paired with the exact predicate phrase or a near-verbatim paraphrase of the question's action or condition.
- Prefer the candidate whose context span contains the exact relation phrase, for example `split in half`, `made of layers of`, or `was tried for`, together with the same class, brand, or descriptive qualifiers supplied by the question, over a more prominent or first-mentioned candidate that appears only near a looser synonym such as `split open` or in a document title or lead.
- Do not let a candidate's high frequency or early position override a second candidate when the second candidate satisfies the exact condition and all supplied class or visual words. Confirm that the selected candidate's class or category term matches the question's everyday category term; association through brand or product family is not enough when the exact action or condition span names a different item.
- Before finalizing, restate the clue with `seen/shown here` and verify that the supporting span uses the same predicate or condition phrase. A near paraphrase is acceptable only when no candidate has the exact phrase.

## Colon-prefixed descriptor prompts with a quoted title are association lookups

- If the text after `Question:` begins with an indefinite descriptor/category (`A [class/role/year genre]`, `An [class]`, etc.) followed by a colon and a quoted title/tagline, do not treat the quoted text as a work title whose creator/director should be returned and do not treat the colon as a delimiter paired answer side unless the source line contains an explicit answer side.
- Treat both the left-hand descriptor and the right-hand quoted phrase as supplied clue material for a missing associated entity. First look for a direct source/adaptation relation attached to the quoted title in the supplied context: `adapted from`, `based on`, `a retelling of`, `adaptation of`, `re-telling of`, `inspired by`, or a defining `... of ...` construction. If a sentence or title line defines the quoted work/title with such a relation, return the named source/original work exactly as written, not the director, creator, cast, medium, year, or quoted title itself.
- If no source/adaptation relation is found, treat the quoted phrase as a possible name-part cue. Collect candidates that match the descriptor/category role and whose proper name shares or is cued by a distinctive word from the quoted phrase (for example a surname matching the quoted term's head word). Prefer that name-part candidate over a person who is merely described as `candidate (Quoted Title)` in a body sentence; that parenthetical credit relation is a distractor when the category/name-part evidence points to another candidate in the same context.
- This overrides the bare titled-work creator-credit rule for this colon-prefixed descriptor format. The bare-title creator-credit and exact answer-side rules apply only when the prompt is a bare `Title (Year)` lookup or a matched delimiter-separated QA record, respectively.

## Dominant prose orthography for proper-name variants

- When a proper name appears in multiple orthographic variants in the supplied context (e.g. hyphenated versus space-separated, accented versus unaccented), do not treat the first variant found in a matching title or parenthetical as the required answer form. Prefer the plain spelling used most consistently in the prose that directly identifies the entity.
- If the question does not itself use the marked variant (such as a hyphen or accent), return the dominant unmarked prose form, even when a directly matching title line uses a marked variant.
- Preserve the chosen form exactly as written in the source. This refines the direct-clue-span preference only for common-name spelling variants; it does not override a matched Jeopardy-style, flashcard, or QA answer side.

## Grammatical-form selection for `this term for ...` definitional slots

- When a definitional prompt says `This term for ...`, `Term for ...`, or a similar phrase and the missing slot is a term name expressed as an action/process phrase (often a gerund or present-participle phrase), choose the context form that grammatically fills that slot rather than defaulting to the shortest dictionary headword or base form.
- If the context contains both a base/headword form and a corresponding present-participle or gerund form used as the name of the concept/title, and the slot asks for the term rather than the bare action word, return the form matching the term slot, including its source capitalization.
- This overrides the headword/base preference for such term-name cloze slots only; it does not replace the dictionary-gloss rule for ordinary definitions of a bare headword.

## Bare place-name lookups prefer administrative location over status-type attributes

- If the text after `Question:` is only a bare place-name, neighborhood, town, city, or geographic area, treat it as an implied location lookup. When the most directly defining context sentence supplies both a status/type predicate (`was a census-designated place`, `is a town`, `was a neighborhood`) and a place hierarchy or location phrase (`in County, State`, `in City, State, Country`), prefer the administrative location attribute from that same sentence over the status/type/classification predicate.
- Return the shortest larger administrative unit directly answering where the place is (state, country, or county) exactly as the source writes it. Do not return a status/type/class label such as `census-designated place`, `neighborhood`, or `unincorporated community` unless the question explicitly asks for the type/status/classification.
- If the source provides only one of these attributes, return that one. If multiple location spans exist, prefer the one in the same sentence that also directly defines the bare place name.

## Quoted trailing title-tail slots prefer the missing head phrase over the full title

- When the text after `Question:` supplies a descriptive noun phrase whose blank/head is identified by a demonstrative or relational clause and appends a quoted trailing title component such as `of [Place]`, `in [Place]`, or `on [Topic]`, treat the quoted trailing component as already supplied clue material. Locate the full source title/phrase that contains that trailing component, then return only the missing subject/head noun phrase that precedes it, exactly as written in the source, including any leading article that belongs to that head phrase.
- Do not return the full title, and do not apply quoted-fragment-full-title expansion when the question's slot is the referent inside the phrase rather than the containing work or full proper title. The quoted tail is removable in this syntactic pattern because the question itself already supplies that tail outside the blank.
- Apply this carve-out only when the quoted tail is grammatically attached as a modifier to the missing noun phrase. When the question explicitly asks for the full title, work, series, or official name, return the full title.

## Singular base term for plural descriptively phrased concept clues

- When a declarative or Jeopardy-style clue identifies a general phenomenon or class by a plural descriptive phrase such as `these [class]s`, `those [class]s`, or another plural `these/those` phrase that is not a proper-name plural slot, treat the plural phrase as supplied clue material rather than as a command to pluralize the answer.
- Locate the context sentence that directly defines or equates the concept with a singular base form (`An X is...`, `X is...`, `called X`, or `known as...`) and return that singular base form exactly as written, even if nearby sentences use the same term in the plural.
- Do not apply this to plural proper-noun or place-name slots such as `these mountains`, `these islands`, or `these lakes`, which should preserve their plural/nominal context form, nor to singular demonstrative class slots (`this fruit`, `this crop`) governed by the separate plural-source preservation rule.
- If the prompt explicitly asks for multiple named instances or a plural class of named examples under the prior plural demonstrative category-member extraction section, retain the plural form from the directly defining source span.

## Short standalone work titles over translated/colon-expanded full titles

- When a question refers to a work through an informal title or title-character clue (`this recent film/book/show`, `the title character of this film`, `this [medium]`), and the supplied context gives both a shorter standalone/original title and a longer colon-separated translated subtitle or alternate title, return the shorter standalone title exactly as written in the direct source span.
- Do not expand a parenthetical original title such as `(Title: Original Title)` into the fuller page title `Title: Subtitle` just because the fuller form is the document heading or first defining line. The subtitle or translated form is required only when the prompt explicitly asks for the full, formal, official, or alternate title.
- If the context contains a direct short form with an original-title label, prefer that labeled original/base form. Preserve source capitalization and spelling; do not add translated title components from headings or another snippet.

## Leading-ellipsis quoted-fragment completion takes missing-prefix priority

- If the text after `Question:` is only a quoted phrase beginning with an ellipsis and ending in a shared suffix fragment (for example `...<tail>`), do not apply the usual quoted-fragment-to-full-proper-noun pointer rule that returns the whole containing phrase, and do not apply title-fragment/source-owner association lookup.
- Treat the fragment after the ellipsis as already supplied clue text. The leading ellipsis marks the omitted prefix as the answer slot. Search the supplied context for a contiguous span that completes the fragment as the tail of a longer fixed phrase, proper title, or proper name, and return only the omitted leading component exactly as written.
- A standalone title or name that equals the fragment is a distractor: it does not supply the missing prefix, and its creator, artist, owner, source, or main title should not be returned for such a leading-ellipsis completion.
- If multiple full phrases end with the same suffix, prefer the one used contiguously in a directly identifying body sentence or title line, especially when the omitted leading component is a proper noun or named entity and that same span identifies it directly. A body sentence that repeats the full phrase is stronger evidence than a document heading or standalone title that contains only the fragment.
- Return only the omitted leading span, preserving source capitalization and spelling. Do not include the quoted suffix, its punctuation, the whole completed phrase, or a creator/artist/owner.

## Additional success patterns for offense labels, term-origin lookups, successor-state names, quoted lyric/passage titles, and inverse former-name fragments

### Offense/crime/sin answer slots

- When the prompt asks for the offense, crime, sin, charge, violation, or similar label for which a named person or character is condemned, punished, sentenced, shunned, or forced to wear/display something, treat the named person, the class word `crime/sin/offense`, and the punishment detail as supplied clue material.
- Do not resolve the pro-form `It` to the named person, the punishment token, or the displayed symbol when the wording is `It's the crime/sin/offense for which ...`; the slot is the offense label itself.
- Locate the source sentence that directly states the relation, for example `PERSON is condemned for committing X`, `PERSON's punishment for X`, or `the crime for which PERSON is condemned ... X`, and return the bare offense/crime/sin term exactly as written in that defining sentence.
- Do not return `committing X`, `the crime of X`, `the sin of X`, a longer punishment description, or the punishment token. Remove any class word already supplied by the question, such as `crime`, `sin`, `offense`, `charge`, or `violation`, while preserving source spelling and capitalization.

### Term/headword extraction for `this term for ...` and `It's said this term ...` origin/definition clues

- When the prompt asks for a term or expression through a definition plus origin, etymology, domain, or date, treat the definition and origin/context details as clue material, not as the answer.
- Locate the supplied context sentence or headword entry that directly equates the term with that definition and origin/context, and return the headword/term exactly as written.
- Do not return the origin person, athlete, place, sport, date, or explanatory narrative when the slot is the term itself. A named person associated with the origin is evidence for the etymology, not the requested term; use the term whose definition and origin constraints match the prompt.
- For action/process term-name slots where the same context offers both a base headword and a gerund/present-participle term name, apply the failure-priority Grammatical-form selection for `this term for ...` definitional slots rule instead of defaulting to the shorter base headword.

### Current/successor and inverse former/alternate-name completion

- When the prompt states that a former, proposed, unrecognized, or earlier named entity became part of, was incorporated into, or formed the nucleus of `this new [state/country/territory/region] in YEAR`, treat the former/proposed entity name, the category word, and the year as supplied clue material.
- Find the source sentence that directly utters the completion, such as `... became part of the new state of X`, `... became the state of X`, or `the area once FORMER became part of X`, and return only the proper-name complement `X` exactly as written.
- Omit supplied category or relational nouns such as `state of`, `territory of`, `part of the new state`, or `new state` when reconstructing the blank; do not return the former entity, the year, or a broader administrative term unless the prompt explicitly asks for it.
- If the text after `Question:` is a truncated or ellipsized fragment that supplies an old, former, alternate, or colloquial name after `as`, `formerly`, `once called`, `originally known as`, or a similar comparative phrase (for example `... as the U.S. holiday X` or `... formerly called X`), treat the supplied old/alternate name as clue material and reconstruct the missing subject as the current/canonical entity. Find the source sentence that directly predicates the supplied old/alternate name of a subject, such as `X was originally called Y`, `X, formerly known as Y`, or `this holiday ... as Y`, and return that subject exactly as written.
- Do not return the old/alternate name itself, a category word, or a document title. If multiple entities share the old/alternate name, use any class, location, date, role, or other qualifier present in the fragment to select the one directly supported by context. This applies even when the fragment begins with `...` and lacks an explicit interrogative word; the completion slot is implied by the fragment.
- For a leading-ellipsis quoted fragment that asks for the omitted prefix of a longer fixed phrase or proper name, apply the Leading-ellipsis quoted-fragment completion takes missing-prefix priority rule instead of this inverse former-name completion. This section applies only where the supplied old/alternate name is a predicate complement and the missing slot is the current/canonical subject.

### Quoted lyric/passage identification returns the containing work/title

- When the prompt identifies a work through quoted lines or passages and a work-level constraint such as a year, medium, chart status, album, show, or film pattern, treat the quoted words and the work-level constraint as clue material for a containing named work/title.
- First search the supplied context for a title/heading or body sentence that directly co-occurs with the quoted lines and the stated constraint, such as `TITLE - YEAR`, `TITLE contains ...`, or a source line that gives the work title adjacent to the lyrics/passage text. Return that title exactly as written.
- Do not return the quoted lines themselves, the performer/author/speaker, the album, the year, or the medium unless the prompt explicitly asks for one of those. If both a short title and a longer formal title appear, prefer the title form used in the sentence that also carries the quoted lines and the given work-level constraint.

## Definitional type-of-this-material or class extraction

- When a clue has the form `X is a type/variety/form of this [material/class]` or `... a synthetic type of this [material/class]`, do not return the named item X, its definitional clause, or an unrelated document title. Locate the most direct context sentence that classifies X through a definitional or equivalence phrase such as `X is a family of synthetic Ys`, `X is a Y`, `a type of Y`, or `a synthetic Y material`, and return the base class noun Y exactly as written there.
- If the question already supplies the classifier word (`material`, `type`, `class`, `substance`, etc.) outside the answer slot, remove that supplied word from the extracted phrase and return only the missing discriminator/base term. Do not append a supplied or entailed head noun such as `material` after the base term.
- Prefer the definition/classification sentence over a document title, heading, or a nearby list that only repeats X. Preserve exact source capitalization, singular/plural form, and any article required for the completed count-noun slot.

## Direct relational-tie and co-participant person extraction

- When a clue names one person and supplies a family, professional, membership, or other role relation along with the missing role label (`child of Y and this playwright`, `successor of X`, `author of Y`, `creator of Y`), treat the named person and the relation/role as clue material rather than as the answer.
- Locate the context sentence that directly ties both people through that exact relation and return the missing person's full canonical name exactly as written in that sentence, such as `Given Surname` or `Honorific Given Surname`.
- When a work, group, or event clue names one participant and asks for the missing co-participant through forms such as `X & this actor`, `X and this [role/person]`, `alongside this [role]`, or `with this [role]`, treat the named participant and the shared action, work, or event as required constraints. Locate the context span that directly places the named participant and the missing person in the same relation or action for the same work/event, and return the missing person's canonical name exactly as written in that span.
- Use the name form from the directly matching span. If that span supplies a full canonical given-and-surname or honorific form, return that full form rather than a surname-only, nickname-only, or truncated form from a separate flashcard/title line. If the directly matching span uses only a short/surname/nickname form, keep that exact form unless the prompt explicitly asks for a full/formal/official name or the direct span itself uses the longer form. This does not override exact answer-side precedence for a matched delimiter-separated quiz or flashcard record.
- Do not return the already-named person, the relationship/role word, an actor or name that merely appears nearby, or a person who shares a role only in another work without satisfying the shared action or work. The requested slot is the other party in the direct relation and must satisfy all named constraints.

## Landmark/event place-slot extraction

- When a clue asks for a place with a demonstrative and administrative class word (`this city`, `this state`, `this country`, `this region`) and supplies a landmark, institution, event, venue, or local feature, treat the supplied landmark/event/feature as clue material, not the answer.
- Locate the context sentence that names the landmark/event/feature together with the requested place or directly places the landmark in that jurisdiction, and return the place proper noun exactly as written there.
- Do not return the landmark/event/feature itself, the state/country when the slot asks for the city, or a different place merely appearing nearby. If the clue includes an enclosing jurisdiction as a constraint (`this [State] city`), require the candidate place to satisfy both the landmark/event and that enclosing state/country in the same or most directly supporting context span.

## Reverse personal-attribute and name-component resolution

- When a declarative or pronoun clue supplies a personal attribute, middle name, known work, membership, or other identifying component (`His/her/its X was Y`, `whose X was Y`, `the X whose Y was Z`) and asks for the person/entity, locate the context sentence that directly equates the supplied attribute to a named entity and return that entity's name exactly as used in that sentence.
- Do not return the supplied attribute, the value Y, a class word, or a document heading. If the directly equating sentence uses an initialized or abbreviated name form, keep that exact form rather than expanding it to a more formal full name from another snippet, unless the prompt explicitly asks for the full/formal/official name.
- If multiple name forms exist, prefer the form inside the sentence that directly states the supplied attribute/relation. Preserve exact capitalization, spelling, punctuation, and source form.

## Supplied examples or parallel instances to shared class, type, or missing paired member

- If the prompt supplies two or more named examples and asserts that they are `varieties/types/kinds of this [singular/plural class]`, do not answer with one of the named examples or a broader container. The examples are clue material for the missing class noun. Locate the source sentence that classifies or lists those examples under the requested common-noun category and return that category term exactly as written, omitting any class word already supplied by the prompt unless it is part of a fixed phrase.
- If a declarative or Jeopardy-style clue gives two or more distinct events, places, productions, or items and asks what `these` or `those` have in common (for example `Event A and Event B had species of these as mascots`, or `X and Y both have this type of Z`), treat every named instance as a required constraint, not as the answer. Locate source spans that assign the same class, species, category, type, or source term to each named instance and return that shared term exactly as written in the direct source.
- Do not return one instance's specific mascot, name, location, or example.
- Before finalizing, restate the clue as the named examples or events each having or being `X` as `Y` and verify that the chosen candidate is directly supported for every named instance.
- If the prompt supplies a relation/event and one of the paired members, then asks for the other member via `this [descriptor]`, such as `between A & this [place/entity]` or `include A & this [descriptor]'s B`, locate the same context sentence that co-locates both members in that relation. Return only the missing member exactly as written, without repeating the supplied member or the descriptive category/relation word.
- This generalizes existing possessive team/city-owner slot rules to non-possessive paired relations. Do not let a nearby heading or a different entity that merely co-occurs with the predicate override the directly paired span.

## Broad class-slot extraction for relational and locational demonstratives

- When a clue has the shape `X was a relative/type/example of this [broad class] found in [place]`, treat the slot as the broad everyday class noun phrase, not a formal, regional, species, or proper-noun compound that shares the same base term.
- Collect both the full source variants and the plain singular/plural common-noun phrase. Prefer the plain common-noun phrase that directly completes the demonstrative slot, including a leading article when the source's directly matching sentence uses one. A compound such as `Regional/Subspecies X` is over-extracted unless the prompt explicitly asks for a formal, official, species, or subspecies name.
- Do not let a proper-noun variant in a heading, lead sentence, or the same paragraph override the short common-noun phrase when the question's slot is a broad class with a locational or relational predicate.
- Before finalizing, insert the candidate into the slot and verify it is not already supplied elsewhere in the question as a class/modifier word. Preserve the exact singular/plural, article, spelling, and capitalization of the chosen source span.

## Bare quoted slogan/catchphrase resolves to a named entity, not its class/type

- If the text after `Question:` is only a quoted slogan, campaign phrase, catchphrase, tagline, or similar quoted key with no explicit question word or blank, treat the quoted text as supplied clue material.
- Do not return a class/type/descriptor such as `campaign slogan`, `song`, `nickname`, `slogan`, `hit`, or a broad genre/medium term when the supplied context directly attaches the quoted phrase to a named person, organization, brand, work, or other entity. The class term is only correct when the prompt explicitly asks for the class/type or when no named attachment exists in the context.
- If a context sentence or paired line equates the quoted phrase with a named entity through language such as `was a campaign slogan for X`, `slogan/catchphrase used by X`, `KEY - PERSON`, or a line-body pairing where the quoted key is followed by a name, first collect every named entity directly attached. If the clue names no particular office/role constraint and multiple associated people are listed, prefer the first/principal named entity from the directly defining span and return its canonical name exactly as written. If the quoted key is a matched Jeopardy-style, flashcard, or delimited QA clue with an explicit answer side, that answer side remains authoritative and should be returned exactly as written.
- Preserve the answer side's capitalization, spelling, article, and number exactly. Do not expand to a full formal name unless the prompt explicitly asks for it or the matched answer side is truncated.

## `in this [place-class]` event clues return the place, not the event title

- When the question has the shape `The [year/event/conference/work] in this [city/state/country/region] ...`, the demonstrative slot is the place-class noun after `this`, not the event or work named earlier in the sentence.
- Locate the context span that directly locates the named event or action at/in/near the place, and return only that place proper noun exactly as written. Do not return a full event title such as `Place Event`, `Place Conference`, or the name of the event already supplied as descriptive material.
- Do not add the event/object class word already present in the question. If the prompt instead says `this conference` or `this event`, then the event name may be the slot; but when the slot is syntactically `this [place-class]`, the place alone is required.
- Before finalizing, replace the slot with the candidate: `The [year] conference in this [city] ...` must be completed by the city name, not by `[City] Conference`. Preserve capitalization and spelling from the source.

## Informal credited-artist and creator clues prefer the shortest directly credited form

- When the text after `Question:` asks for a person through an informal work-credit relation such as `Artist whose ...`, `Painter of ...`, `Composer who wrote ...`, `Director of ...`, or `Creator of ...`, and the supplied context contains both a short credited form (surname, common name, or nickname) and a fuller canonical given-name form, treat the prompt as an informal credit lookup, not as a formal or status/office identification.
- Locate the context sentence that directly states the credit relation together with the work or style/period in the prompt, such as `[Work] by [Name]`, `... by [Name] in the [style] period`, `[Name], [Work]`, or `[Work] is an example of [style]` near the credited name. Return the exact name form used in that directly matching sentence, even if it is a bare surname or short common form.
- Do not expand to a fuller given-name form from slide lines, headings, captions, or separate encyclopedic sentences merely because that fuller form also appears in the supplied context. A full slide or caption form is correct only when the prompt explicitly asks for a full/formal/official name or when the direct predicate sentence itself uses that fuller form.
- This overrides the general `Person-name canonical form over terse answer records` preference for informal `Artist/Painter/Creator of X` work-credit clues. It does not override exact answer-side precedence for a matched Jeopardy-style, flashcard, or delimited QA record, and it does not apply to clues requesting an office-holder, honoree, official status, or relational title that require the full canonical name.
- Before finalizing, restate the clue as `This is a [work/style] by whom?` and verify the candidate is the shortest name form that directly co-occurs with the named work and style/period or other predicate in a single context sentence.

## All-caps flashcard and quiz answer sides normalize to prose case

- When a matched Jeopardy-style, flashcard, delimiter-separated QA, or quiz record has an answer side that is entirely uppercase or stylized because of flashcard/quiz formatting, and surrounding prose, titles, or body sentences supply the same proper name in normal prose case, return the normal prose form rather than the all-caps string.
- This refines exact answer-side precedence only for letter case. Keep terse surname-only, nickname-only, abbreviated, and short title forms from the matched answer side exactly as given, including article and number. Do not expand the answer or import a different form from a distant snippet.
- If no nearby normal-case prose form of the same answer exists, preserve the answer-side capitalization exactly.

## Success-verified closed numeric option sets

- When the prompt begins with `Of A, B, or C, ...` or `Of X, Y or Z, ...`, treat the enumerated tokens as a closed candidate set, including when they are bare numerals, spelled-out numbers, or short numeric ranges. Locate the most directly defining source sentence for the predicate and return the matching candidate exactly as written in the prompt. Do not derive a different numeric value from nearby fact bullets, and do not choose an outside value that is not among the listed candidates; use the surrounding context only to select among the supplied tokens.

## Nation or owner lookup from a named capital, award, or institution

- If the question says `X is the capital of this [descriptor] country/nation`, `This country's [named award/institution] ...`, or an analogous state/city/region possessive slot, treat the named capital, award, or institution as clue material. Locate the context span that directly assigns that named item to its country, state, or owner and return the owner/place name exactly as written.
- If the context contains conflicting rank, size, or superlative descriptions, prefer the country/place tied to the named capital/award in the direct sentence; do not substitute another place merely because it independently satisfies the superlative or class descriptor.
- This extends the existing relational-slot and possessive rules to capital-country, named-award, and institution-owner pairings. Do not return the capital, award, institution, or a broad class/nation label unless the prompt explicitly asks for it.

## Minimal named-complement selection for bare lookup keys

- If the text after `Question:` is only a bare comma-separated list of named entities or a bare `[class] [name]` key with no explicit question word or blank, treat it as an implied-lookup slot. Collect the context sentence or title that directly defines or classifies all listed/named entities.
- If the source offers both a longer relation phrase such as `[Role/Type] of X`, `a [role/type] for X`, or `[Name] | [Role/Type]`, and a shorter named complement `X`, return only `X`, exactly as written. The role/type words are evidence for the relation, not part of the answer, unless the prompt explicitly asks for that role/type/class.
- For a named cover/tribute act preceded only by a broad category word, locate the direct relation such as `... is a tribute to X`, `... was a cover band for X`, `... performs X`, `... models itself on X`, or a title line `[Act] | X Tribute Band`. Return the original/base target `X`, not `X Tribute Band` or the act's descriptive type.
- Before finalizing, restate the implied slot and delete any word already present or entailed in the question (`rock group`, `band`, `tribute`, `king`, `president`, `member`, etc.) from the candidate. A candidate that repeats an unrequested class or role word is over-extracted.
- This does not override exact answer-side precedence for matched Jeopardy-style, flashcard, or QA records. Preserve source spelling, capitalization, and singular/plural form.

## Nickname, alias, and moniker slots return only the bare appellation token

- When a question asks for a nickname, alias, moniker, `better known moniker`, popular name, or similar appellation for an already named person, that wording is an explicit request for the appellation token only. Complete the slot with the bare nickname/alias token, not with `Nickname Surname`, not with the person's legal/full formal name, and not with a title or role.
- Even if the supplied context repeatedly spells the same person as `Nickname Surname` or uses that compound as a heading, document title, or caption, do not import the following surname or legal name when the clue asks specifically for the moniker. The subject identity is already supplied in the prompt; only the alias discriminator is missing.
- Select from the most directly defining equivalence or answer record: `known as`, `widely known as`, `better known as`, `nickname is`, `also known as`, a labeled `Nickname:` line, or a matched quiz/flashcard answer side. Return the exact token as written in that record. If the direct answer side or defining equivalence presents the nickname in quotation marks, preserve that quoted token exactly, including the quotation marks, as an exception to the default no-quotation-mark extraction rule. Do not extend it to a later `Nickname Surname` form from prose or headings.
- Before finalizing, insert the candidate into the completed slot phrase, such as `X's better known moniker is ___` or `X's nickname is ___`, and verify that it fills only the moniker token. If the candidate repeats part of the subject's legal name or surname, reduce it to the appellation token extracted from the direct equivalence or answer span.
- This overrides canonical-name and full proper-noun expansion for moniker/nickname slots only. It does not change exact answer-side precedence for matched quiz/flashcard records except to forbid repeating the subject's surname when the requested slot is the bare moniker.

## Facility/place slots require body-sentence relation, not title-label candidates

- When a declarative or cloze prompt supplies an entity/activity, a date or date range, and a demonstrative place slot such as `this [place/facility/base]` with a trailing locative descriptor, treat the place as the missing answer and treat the entity/activity/date plus locative descriptor as required constraints.
- Collect candidate place names from body sentences that directly tie the same entity/activity/date to the location through locative or relational language (`at`, `from`, `in`, `near`, `assembly took place at`, `final assembly is at`, etc.).
- Do not select a candidate solely because a document title or heading is a place-name-like label and the same snippet shares the locative descriptor and entity words. A title labels the source snippet; it does not by itself establish that the titled place is the location of the entity/activity/date in the prompt.
- If the body under such a title does not directly assert the requested location relation, reject the title candidate. If another body sentence does directly assert that relation and names a place, prefer that body-sentence place over any title candidate.
- Before finalizing, insert the candidate into the prompt and verify that the resulting statement is directly supported by a body sentence, not reconstructed from a title plus topical overlap.

## Informal pronoun/office-holder person clues: prefer the shortest complete direct name over formal middle-initial/full variants

- When a declarative or demonstrative person clue uses a pro-form or informal role phrase (`this president`, `she...`, `he...`, `the man who...`) with a dated action, quote, or event, treat it as informal identification, not a request for an official or formal full name.
- If the supplied context contains two or more name forms for the same person, such as `Given Surname`, `Given MiddleInitial Surname`, and `Given MiddleName Surname`, prefer the shortest complete first-name-plus-surname form that is directly attached to the same dated action, quote, or event.
- Do not import a middle initial or middle name from a different document title, caption, or formal official line when the directly supporting sentence or a co-occurring source line gives the shorter two-word name. A longer formal variant is needed only when the question already includes that middle component, explicitly asks for a full/formal/official name, or no shorter complete first-last form is available.
- This overrides general canonical-name expansion for informal pro-form/date/quote clues. Preserve exact source spelling and capitalization.

## Company/organization name reduction from paraphrased industry-class slots

- If a demonstrative identification slot uses a paraphrased industry or category phrase (for example `this satellite radio company`, `this restaurant chain`, or `this software firm`) and the supplied context gives a longer company/entity name that repeats the same descriptive category words as part of its official-looking name, treat those repeated category words as supplied clue material.
- Remove the redundant industry/classification suffix from the candidate even when the source capitalizes it inside the name. Return only the shortest distinguishing proper-name portion that can complete the slot: `this satellite radio company` should get `X`, not `X Satellite Radio`, unless the question explicitly asks for the full official, corporate, or legal name or for a full fixed title.
- Do not let the fact that the longer form is a proper noun in the source override the supplied-category reduction. A fuller corporate/descriptive name is over-extracted if its tail restates the question's class words.
- Preserve source capitalization and spelling of the retained proper-name portion.

## Bare named-person/entity lists prefer a single named common attribute over third-party relations

- When the text after `Question:` is only a bare conjunction/separator list of named entities (for example `Name1 & Name2`) with no explicit question word, blank, or category noun, collect every context span that assigns the same simple attribute to all listed names: a place/location, affiliation, country/region, team, company, owner, parent, or other named attribute.
- Prefer the shortest single named attribute value from a direct context sentence, especially when that value appears as the location/affiliation complement in the entities' own source names or titles (such as `X of Place` / `Y of Place`). Return that value exactly as written and do not include the preposition or class word unless it is part of a fixed name.
- Do not return a relational clause into a third named entity (for example `siblings of Person Z`, `children of Person Z`, or `members of Group G`) when the prompt does not explicitly ask for that relationship. A family or membership relation is evidence for identifying the named list, but the implied answer slot should be the common named attribute itself.
- If multiple common attributes are supported, prefer a named place/location or institution complement over a predictive relationship clause, and prefer the shortest source span that directly pairs all listed names with the same attribute.

## Original/base title over altered, punning, or derived forms

- When the question states that a modified, punning, adapted, or derived title or phrase was created by changing or replacing one word or segment of an original (patterns such as `changed "X" to "Y" in this original title`, `a spoof/adaptation of TITLE`, or `taken from TITLE`), treat the modified/derived form as supplied clue material, not as the answer.
- Locate the context sentence that explicitly equates the modified form with its source through relation words such as `changed ... to`, `taken from`, `based on`, `adapted from`, `derived from`, or `also used as`, and return the original/base title or phrase exactly as written in that sentence.
- Do not return the modified/pun form, the adaptation title, or a heading/list item that only displays the modified title. A derived form containing the changed word is a distractor when the question asks for the original/canonical title.
- If the question uses `this` plus a category word such as `title`, `original title`, `source work`, or `work`, use that category to select the base title from the defining relation, not the adapted counterpart that co-occurs in the same context.
- Before finalizing, restate the relation as `Altered form was created from this original ___` and verify that the candidate is the source/base form, not the altered or derived form.

## Matched quiz/flashcard answer-side reduction for supplied class heads

- When an exact or near-verbatim Jeopardy-style, flashcard, delimiter-separated QA, or quiz record matches the question, use the matched answer side to identify the target, but before finalizing insert it into the question's explicit or implicit slot. If the question already supplies a class/category head noun through a demonstrative such as `this [class]`, `that [class]`, or `these [class]s`, remove that same class/category word from the answer side. Exact answer-side precedence protects terse proper names, person names, and work titles; it does not justify repeating a class word that is already present in the question.
- When the reduced answer completes a singular definite or count phrase, supply the article required by the completed slot (`a`/`an` for an indefinite singular count phrase, `the` for a definite singular/plural phrase), using the closest source/prose form of the completed phrase when available. Do not leave an ungrammatical bare modifier if the completed slot requires an article.
- If the matched answer side is entirely uppercase or stylized only because of quiz/flashcard formatting, normalize it to the prose case used in the surrounding context while keeping the reduced span.
- Example pattern: a question asks for `this [class]` and a matching answer side is `[modifier] [class]`; return the missing discriminator plus any required article, not the full `[modifier] [class]` phrase.
- Before finalizing, replace the demonstrative with the candidate and verify that the class word is not repeated. Preserve spelling and capitalization after case normalization.

## Pronoun-resolved Jeopardy and cloze clues prefer the shortest directly attested name form

- If a declarative or Jeopardy-style clue uses a personal or possessive pronoun (`his`, `her`, `their`, `he`, `she`) or an informal demonstrative pro-form and does not explicitly request a full/formal/official name, resolve the pronoun to the identified referent and return the shortest well-attested name or title form used in a context span that directly mirrors the clue predicate.
- This applies especially when the supplied context contains a category-labeled quiz line without an answer side. Treat that quiz line as ordinary cloze evidence, then use a nearby title, heading, or directly matching body sentence that pairs the same predicate with a short name form (for example `Name defeated at X`, `Name's final defeat at X`) as the answer form.
- A longer canonical form in a separate summary or lead sentence (for example `the defeat and second abdication of Full Given Surname`) is supporting evidence for identity, but it must not override the shorter predicate-matching form unless the prompt explicitly asks for a full/formal/official name, an office-holder title, or another status requiring canonical completeness.
- Before finalizing, restate the completed clue as an answer line. If the source's most direct answer-like phrase, title, or heading supplies a shorter name, keep that shorter form exactly as written. Do not expand it merely because a fuller form appears elsewhere in the supplied context.

## Full fixed name completion for conjunction and ampersand blanks

- When a fill-in-the-blank or cloze prompt supplies one member of a fixed proper noun joined by `&`, `and`, or another coordinating conjunction (for example `___ & Y`, `X & ___`, `___ and Y`), treat the blank as part of a fixed proper name or partnership title, not as a removable class/location word.
- Locate the source context span that contains the complete fixed phrase and return the entire proper noun exactly as written there, including the already supplied member and the conjunction. Do not reduce the answer to only the missing component.
- If the context contains both `&` and `and` forms, prefer the full source form whose conjunction and spelling match the prompt's supplied surroundings.
- Slot-refilling reduction removes only supplied category, location, or class nouns outside proper names. It must not remove the supplied tail/head of a fixed proper noun or official partnership title.
- Preserve exact capitalization, spelling, punctuation, and spacing from the selected source span.

## Exact orthographic form for acronym and initialism expansions

- When the question supplies a short marker, acronym, or initialism and asks what feature or term it names, locate the context sentence that directly expands or equates the marker with its long form (for example the phrase immediately before a parenthetical initialism, or a definition line of the form `long form (MARKER)`). Return that direct expansion exactly as written in that same sentence.
- If the context contains multiple orthographic variants of the same term, such as an open compound `X in Y` and a hyphenated compound `X-in-Y`, prefer the variant from the directly defining or equating sentence over variants in unrelated headlines, titles, or later snippets.
- Do not normalize hyphenation, spacing, capitalization, or punctuation between variants. Exact-match evaluation depends on returning the exact source form.
- This applies to definitional acronym or initialism lookups; it does not override exact answer-side precedence for matched Jeopardy-style, flashcard, or delimiter-separated QA records.

## Supplemental success-derived clue-resolution patterns

### Inverse possession and favorite-object slots return the owner/person
- When a declarative or cloze clue supplies a named object, tool, device, item, or creation as `the favorite X of this [role/descriptor]`, `the X of this [person/place]`, or another inverted possession relation, treat the supplied object as clue material. Locate the context sentence that directly assigns that object to its named owner, user, or associated person, and return the owner/person exactly as written.
- The slot is the missing possessor/owner, not the object and not a broader category word. Use all role, period, place, or action modifiers in the question to select the correct person. Prefer the context snippet that directly pairs the object with the same descriptors, such as `[Person] had a [thing] that was known as the '[name]'` or `[Person] ... his favorite [thing]`.
- This extends the existing creator/source and possessive-team rules to generic favorite-item, instrument, apparel, weapon, or possession pairings. Preserve exact source spelling and capitalization.

### Impostor and assumed-identity slots return the person whose identity was borrowed
- If a prompt names a person and says that person gained access, became infamous, or inspired a work by `posing as`, `claiming to be`, or `convincing others they were` `this [role]'s [relative]`, or describes an `ersatz/spurious [relative]` of an unnamed person, the missing slot is the borrowed identity, not the impostor or the relative label.
- Locate the context sentence that directly ties the named impostor to the assumed identity through wording such as `posing as [X]'s son`, `convincing them he was [X]'s son`, `the ersatz son of [X]`, or similar, and return the identity-holder `X` exactly as written.
- If multiple spellings appear, use the spelling from the most directly defining sentence or the dominant prose form. Do not return a co-mentioned alternative relative or a person who merely appears nearby.
- This refines the possessive-demonstrative rule: in a possessive relative phrase such as `this actor's son`, the possessor is the missing slot because the relative and the impostor are already supplied as clue material.

### Inverse named-for/honoree resolution when the named object is supplied
- When the prompt supplies a named object, place, studio, award, or institution and says it is `named for`, `named after`, or `named in honor of` a missing person or descriptive slot such as `this late journalist`, `this [role/nationality]`, or `her`/`him`, the missing slot is the honoree/person, not the named object.
- Find the sentence that directly states the naming relation and return the person's canonical name exactly as written there, following the person-name canonical-form rule unless an exact matched quiz/flashcard answer side takes precedence.
- This is the inverse of the existing reverse-naming rule: when the honoree is supplied and the named entity is missing, still return the named entity; when the named entity is supplied and the honoree/person is missing, return the person.

### Bare descriptive common-noun prompts are implied lookups for the defining equivalent term
- If the text after `Question:` is only an article plus a descriptive common-noun or class phrase, such as `An Anglican parish priest`, `A ...`, with no explicit question word, blank, or demonstrative slot, do not return that input phrase, a broader class label, or a heading that merely repeats the phrase.
- Treat the phrase as clue material for an implied equivalence lookup. Locate the directly defining or classifying context sentence and return the shortest specific equivalent role/title/term from that sentence, for example from wording such as `is usually called`, `is also called`, `is`, or a definitional appositive.
- If the context gives two coordinate equivalents, prefer the one from the sentence that directly defines the full supplied phrase and matches every qualifier; when both are equal, return the first direct equivalent spelled exactly in that defining sentence. Do not add a class word already supplied in the prompt unless it is part of the fixed term.
- This extends the earlier bare-term and implied-slot rule to descriptive common-noun prompts. It does not apply to bare proper names, bare comma-separated named-entity lists, or titled-work lookups.

### Name-meaning and translated-name reverse lookup
- When the prompt states that `the name of this/these [class] means/translates to` a quoted or described word, treat the meaning as already supplied clue material, not as the answer.
- Locate the context span that directly pairs a proper name or headword with that meaning through language such as `means`, `literally`, `translates to`, `in [language]`, or a dictionary-style definition under the name. Return only the named entity, base term, or proper name exactly as written in that span.
- Do not return the quoted meaning, the language, the class/category word, or a different named entity that shares the language but has a different meaning. Prefer the body sentence that contains the exact meaning relation over a distant heading or unrelated definition.

### Presentational copular-definition clues return the predicate noun, not the named brand/place
- If the text after `Question:` is a declarative presentational clue that provides a quoted or descriptive definition of an object and then says it is a `mainstay`, `specialty`, `type`, `example`, or `fixture` of a named brand, chain, region, or institution, treat the named brand/place as supplied clue material. Resolve the missing slot to the base common noun or noun phrase that is directly predicated of that definition in the source.
- Use the source sentence that most directly defines or identifies the object by the same purpose, composition, or presentation, such as `[Brand]'s [answer] may be ...` or `[answer] is ... made with ...`. Return that common-noun head exactly as written, without the named brand/place and without repeating ingredient or class words already supplied by the prompt.
- Do not answer with the brand, chain, place, ingredient list, or a broader category term unless the prompt explicitly asks for the brand or category. This refines the existing definitional shortest-span rule for copular presentational clues.

### Definitional `This phrase describes ...` glossary slots
- If the text after `Question:` is a definitional gloss such as `This phrase describes X`, `This term describes X`, `A phrase for X`, or `The term for X is ...`, treat the descriptive clause as clue material. Find the supplied context sentence that defines a headword/term with that exact or paraphrased description and return only that headword/term phrase exactly as written.
- Do not return the descriptive clause, a neighboring legal label, a document title, or a generic class noun when the source explicitly gives the term as a headword. A context line of the form `Headword definition, <definition>` supports returning the headword, not the definition phrase or a nearby longer title.
- Keep the source's spelling, hyphenation, and capitalization for the headword.

### Multi-sense dictionary gloss prompts
- If the text after `Question:` is a definitional prompt that supplies two or more gloss senses joined by `or`, `or to`, or a comma, treat all listed senses as required matching constraints, not as answer material.
- Collect the supplied dictionary or glossary entries and select the headword/base term whose single entry lists all of those senses. Do not answer with a term that satisfies only one sense or with the gloss words themselves.
- Return the exact base/heading form from that defining entry, and do not switch to a plural or inflected variant unless the direct entry uses that form. This is a refinement of the dictionary-gloss rule for conjoined sense prompts.

### Ignore trailing clue-length and page annotations on quiz-style prompts
- If the text after `Question:` ends with a parenthesized integer or short clue metadata such as `(15)`, `(6)`, or `(5,2)`, and the question is otherwise a full declarative/cloze clue, treat the parenthetical as answer-length, page, or point metadata rather than an answer constraint. Match the clue body against the context and return the entity named by the body.
- Do not return the number, the page, or a context snippet merely because it contains the same number unless the question explicitly asks for that numeric attribute.
- Exception: keep parenthetical years when they are part of a bare titled-work lookup (`Title (Year)`) asking for a creator/director, as covered by the existing bare titled-work rule.

### All-caps flashcard and quiz answer sides normalize to prose case
- When a matched Jeopardy-style, flashcard, delimiter-separated QA, or quiz record has an answer side that is entirely uppercase because of flashcard/quiz formatting, and nearby prose, titles, or body sentences supply the same proper name in normal prose case, return the normal prose form rather than the all-caps string.
- This refines exact answer-side precedence only for letter case. Keep the matched answer side's terse surname-only, nickname-only, abbreviated, and short-title forms exactly as given, including article and number. Do not expand the answer or import a different form from a distant snippet.
- If no nearby normal-case prose form of the same answer exists, preserve the answer-side capitalization exactly.

### Instructional conditional slots
- When a question is phrased as a tip, recipe, or how-to conditional such as `Try mixing X with Y if you run out of this [category]`, `If you don't have this [category], use X`, or `When this [category] is unavailable, ...`, match the supplied-context sentence that states the same practical condition or substitution rather than a topically related sentence.
- Locate the exact procedure span, usually containing `run out of`, `don't have any`, `out of`, or `instead`, and extract the missing object/item noun exactly as written there. Apply supplied-class-word reduction: if the question already says the category noun, return only the missing discriminator.
- Do not return the substitute ingredient, the product named in the tip, or an instruction word. Prefer the most directly matching procedure sentence over document titles or general list paragraphs.

### Possessive property and formula facts as implicit class clues
- If the text after `Question:` is only a declarative property/fact statement whose subject is a possessive pronoun such as `Its`, without an explicit question word or blank, treat the statement as a definitional lookup key, not as a yes/no proposition and not as a formula to return.
- Locate the supplied context sentence that presents the same property or formula as the defining attribute of a category or named entity, and return the base common noun or canonical name that is the subject of that defining sentence, exactly as written.
- Do not return the formula, equation, value, or property words already supplied in the clue.

### Demonstrative place-slot resolution from a dated event or causal relation
- When a declarative or cloze prompt has `this [place class]` together with a dated event or causal relation naming a person, work, or later outcome (`... inspired Y`, `... led to Y`, `... created Y`, `... after the X riots`, etc.), treat the date, participant/outcome, and place-class word as required constraints.
- Locate the body sentence that directly binds the place to that event/causal relation, not a nearby document title or snippet that merely repeats some of the same keywords. Return only the place proper noun exactly as written in that directly supporting sentence.
- Do not return the person, work, outcome, year, or a larger/smaller region unless the prompt asks for it. Omit the supplied place-class word (`neighborhood`, `city`, `district`, `region`, etc.) when extracting.
- Prefer the shortest place name from the same directly binding sentence. Preserve exact source spelling and capitalization.

### Transport-connector geographic clues with numeric lengths
- When the prompt gives a physical connector such as a causeway, bridge, or tunnel, an approximate length or distance, and says it connects or links `this [nation/territory/place]` with a named neighbor or mainland, treat the connector, length, and named neighbor as supplied clue material.
- Match the length approximately across fractions, decimals, and units. Return the place or nation named as the connected entity in the same context span that pairs the connector, length, and neighbor, not the already supplied neighbor and not the connector itself.
- Prefer the sentence or title that directly states both the connector and the candidate place, such as `A [length] causeway connects this [place-class] with [named neighbor]`. Do not select a place solely because it appears elsewhere near a similar connector or length; require direct binding of the connector and named neighbor to the candidate.
- Preserve the place name's exact source spelling and capitalization.

### Fixed-title component completion for descriptor-prefixed proper-name blanks
- When the prompt is a fill-in-the-blank fixed proper name with an optional short descriptor before a colon and a missing component inside an institutional, organizational, or work title, treat the words around the blank as a contiguous template.
- Find the source title or heading that contains the full fixed proper name verbatim or near-verbatim, and return only the missing template component exactly as written there. Do not answer with a broad domain or class word merely because it describes the entity's area of activity.
- Do not include punctuation, the preceding descriptor text, or words already supplied in the prompt. If multiple source forms contain the surrounding words, prefer the span whose surrounding template most closely matches the post-colon phrase.

### Author/year/plot-constrained work-title selection
- When a clue supplies multiple narrative constraints for a created work, such as named groups/characters, a setting, and an author/creator plus a year or medium (`... in this [year] [author] [novel/film/album]`), treat each named group, setting, author/creator, year, and medium as a required constraint.
- Locate the context span that ties the same work title to the author/creator and year, and also supports the described groups/action/setting, then return that work title exactly as written. Prefer the title from a sentence or title line that satisfies all constraints simultaneously over a work that shares only the author, setting, or year.
- Do not return the author, a character group, the setting, or a different work with only a partial keyword match. This extends the existing work-title completion rule beyond award/achievement constraints to ordinary plot, cast, and setting constraints.

edits.content:
## Unpaired quiz/archive clue lines are ordinary cloze prompts

- If the supplied context contains a Jeopardy-style, J! Archive, flashcard, or quiz clue line whose question text appears without a delimiter-separated answer side, treat it as an ordinary `this`/`these` identification or cloze clue even when there is no leading `CATEGORY:` label and no page/category label before the clue.
- Do not require an answer record, and do not return the archive title, page title, show number, or source label as the answer. Use any available category/page label only as an additional class or scope constraint.
- Match the clue predicate against body sentences and matching titles in the supplied context. If the clue contains a superlative or comparative relation such as `greater than all other ...`, `surpasses all previous ...`, or `more than all other ...`, allow the supporting body sentence to express the same comparative relation through a closely related quantitative attribute (for example cost, death toll, size, or rank) when no closer support exists.
- Return the named entity, work, place, or title that satisfies all explicit class and relational constraints, exactly as written in the directly supporting context span. Do not answer with a related but different candidate merely because it appears in the quiz line or source title.

## Implicit candidate-set superlatives under explicit scope conditions

- When a question selects a member from a broad class with a superlative or ordering predicate such as `smallest`, `largest`, `first`, `last`, or `only`, without explicitly enumerating the candidate list, treat the class term and any scope modifier (`currently`, `modern`, `today`, `existing`, `circulating`, `active`) as required constraints.
- Collect only candidates that satisfy the explicit scope condition in the supplied context, then prefer the candidate whose context span directly supports the superlative or ordering relation. Ignore named group members that are historical, discontinued, former, or otherwise outside the stated scope even if they also fit the broad class.
- Return the selected member as the shortest common noun, proper name, or title form from that directly supporting context span. Do not add the class/category word already supplied by the question, and do not choose a broader group term.
- If the completed slot is a count-noun phrase, keep the source's article and singular/plural form when part of the directly matched answer; otherwise prefer the bare noun.

## Parenthetical descriptors after `seen here`/`shown here` in unpaired clue lines

- If the text after `Question:` is an unpaired Jeopardy-style, flashcard, or quiz clue that includes a visual pointer such as `seen here`, `shown here`, `pictured here`, or `appearing here` plus a trailing parenthetical descriptor such as `(U.S. president, '81-'89)`, `(sultan/office)`, or `(film, year)`, do not treat the parenthetical as the answer or as a paired answer side.
- Treat the parenthetical as required role, office, status, date, or medium constraints for resolving the preceding pronoun, noun phrase, or descriptive predicate. Find the candidate in the supplied context whose directly defining sentence satisfies both the predicate and every parenthetical constraint. Return that candidate exactly as written in the most directly satisfying title or body sentence; for a person use the canonical first-name-plus-surname form when the direct span supports it.
- The visual pointer only indicates that the target appears in an image; it does not add a class/slot word to remove. Do not choose a different entity merely because another snippet shares the same title, date, office, or a paraphrased phrase without the direct identity tie.

## Comma-delimited flashcard and QA answer fields

- If the supplied context has a flashcard or QA line of the form `CLUE, ANSWER` with no pipe delimiter, and the text before the comma matches the question clue verbatim or by near paraphrase, treat the first term after the comma as the matched answer side just like an explicit `clue | answer` record.
- Return that answer-side term exactly as written, omitting any further sentence continuation, source-title text, page number, or trailing category/status annotation. Do not import a different name from a nearby body sentence or document title merely because it discusses the same topic.
- If the answer side is a proper name or fixed title, preserve its capitalization, spelling, article, and number from the answer field. This is a comma-delimited case of exact answer-side precedence for matched quiz/flashcard records; it does not override that rule.

## Multi-adjective `this [class]` dictionary-gloss extraction

- When a `this`/`that` identification clue has a class noun preceded by several descriptive adjectives or adjectival phrases (for example `this freshwater eellike, jawless fish`), treat all those modifiers and the class noun as required constraints rather than as part of the answer.
